However, with respect to those who come as refugees, we say we are recognizing a right rather than granting a privilege. We recognize this as a right because we, as a nation, have signed certain international covenants. Where people are in need of refuge, we as a nation that prides itself on a humane tradition, a tradition of fairness and helping those in need, have an obligation to provide that refuge. It is not a privilege we extend but a right that we recognize. The committee agreed with Rabbi Plaut that there should be no distinction between those who have entered Canada legally and those who have entered illegally when it comes to applying for refugee status. who continuing to demand: (i) universal access to a simple, fair and efficient system (ii) an impartial decision making body formed by refugee experts and chosen in consultation with other concerned organizations. (iii) an initial and full hearing (iv) the right to a lawyer of one's choice (v) a full right of appeal (vi) the independence of the refugee system from immigration (vii) equitable treatment of claims made abroad. The Government has never formally rejected these objectives in principle but Bill C-55 denies them. In conclusion, I would urge the Government to withdraw Bill C-55 and bring in a Bill which would eliminate the abuse, provide for a shorter appeal process, but still provide for a full and fair hearing for refugee claimants so that Canada will continue to be a country that can hold its head high when it looks at the whole refugee situation throughout our world.
